claim: A reference genome for European blackcaps was assembled with a length of 1.02 Gb, comprised of 96 scaffolds, and an N50 scaffold length of 22 Mb.
source: The final genome is 1.02 Gb in length, comprised of only 96 scaffolds and has a large N50 scaffold length of 22 Mb.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the assembly statistics including genome size, scaffold number, and N50 length.

claim: Ninety scaffolds from the blackcap genome mapped to the collared flycatcher genome with an average of three scaffolds per chromosome.
source: Ninety scaffolds mapped to the collared flycatcher Ficedula albicollis genome (average three scaffolds/chromosome; Supplementary file 3)
evidence: The manuscript reports mapping results between blackcap and flycatcher genomes.

claim: The blackcap genome annotation identified 17,982 protein-coding genes.
source: our annotation strategy, which used both in silico and evidence-based approaches, identified 17,982 protein-coding genes.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of protein-coding genes identified through annotation.

claim: The blackcap reference genome is nearly complete with 92% of single-copy orthologues unique to birds and 97% of UCEs identified in amniotes.
source: Results from BUSCO and an analysis of UCEs (ultra-conserved elements) suggest that our reference is nearly complete, with 92% of single-copy orthologues unique to birds and 97% of UCEs identified in amniotes (Faircloth et al., 2012; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports BUSCO and UCE analysis results as measures of genome completeness.

claim: Whole genome resequencing data was obtained from 110 blackcaps with an average coverage of 17.5x.
source: We aligned WGS data from 110 blackcaps (including the two birds used in our assembly) to this reference (average coverage 17.5x, Figure 1a, Supplementary file 4)
evidence: The manuscript directly states the sample size and sequencing coverage.

claim: Genomic differentiation was low between migratory populations of different distances and orientations.
source: Genomic differentiation was low between migratory populations of different distances and orientations, but unlike earlier work using mitochondrial data (Pérez-Tris et al., 2004; Dietzen et al., 2008), we documented considerable differentiation between migrant and resident populations on both the continent and islands.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and contrasts it with previous mitochondrial studies.

claim: Considerable genomic differentiation exists between migrant and resident blackcap populations on both the continent and islands.
source: Genomic differentiation was low between migratory populations of different distances and orientations, but unlike earlier work using mitochondrial data (Pérez-Tris et al., 2004; Dietzen et al., 2008), we documented considerable differentiation between migrant and resident populations on both the continent and islands.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding based on genome-wide data.

claim: Principal component analysis separated resident island birds from continental populations on PC1, and resident continental birds from migrants on PC2.
source: A PCA separated resident island birds from continental populations on PC1, and resident continental birds from migrants on PC2 (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript describes PCA results and references Figure 1b showing the separation.

claim: FST estimates between blackcap populations ranged from 0.018 to 0.11, with the highest estimates occurring between migrants and both resident groups.
source: Estimates of FST ranged from 0.018 to 0.11, with the highest estimates occurring between migrants and both resident groups (0.06–0.11 for islands, 0.042–0.05 for continent residents; Figure 1d).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific FST values and their distribution across population comparisons.

claim: The demographic trajectories of migratory, resident continent and resident island blackcaps began to diverge approximately 30,000 years ago.
source: The demographic trajectories of migratory, resident continent and resident island birds began to diverge ~30,000 ya.
evidence: The manuscript states this timing based on MSMC2 demographic analysis.

claim: Divergence of blackcap populations began approximately 30,000 years ago at the start of the last glacial maximum.
source: Our results move this date further back in time, to 30,000 ya and the start of the last glacial maximum (Clark et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this timing and links it to the last glacial maximum.

claim: The effective population size of migrant blackcaps expanded while that of resident island populations contracted, and continental residents exhibited a relatively constant effective population size.
source: The effective population size of migrant and resident island populations expanded and contracted, respectively, while continental residents exhibited a relatively constant effective population size (Figure 2a; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes demographic trajectories based on MSMC2 analysis and references supporting figures.

claim: Relative cross-coalescence rates between all three blackcap groups exhibited a drop approximately 30,000 years ago.
source: Relative cross-coalescence rates (CCR) between all three groups exhibited a concomitant drop ~30,000 ya (Figure 2b; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports CCR results from MSMC2 analysis.

claim: The drop in relative cross-coalescence rate between migratory and resident island populations was steeper than that between migratory and resident continent populations.
source: The drop of relative CCR between migratory and resident island populations was steeper than that between migratory and resident continent populations (Figure 2b), suggesting that genetic separation following the colonization of islands resulted in greater separation than that between continental populations of migrants and residents.
evidence: The manuscript describes differences in CCR patterns and provides an interpretation.

claim: Gene flow occurred between migrant and resident continent blackcaps approximately 5,000 years ago.
source: One interesting finding from our demographic analyses is that of apparent gene flow between migrant and resident continent birds ~5000 years ago. Specifically, the relative CCR between migrant and resident continent populations started to increase at ~5000 ya (~25,000 years after initial divergence; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports evidence of gene flow based on CCR analysis.

claim: Nine genomic regions were found to be under selection according to hapFLK analysis, with six of these appearing in resident populations.
source: Only nine regions were found to be under selection (permutation test, see 'Materials and methods') according to this method, and six of these appeared in residents.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number and distribution of regions under selection from hapFLK analysis.

claim: The average size of genomic regions under selection identified by hapFLK was 16.7 kb.
source: The average size of these regions was 16.7 kb and only six genes occurred within them.
evidence: The manuscript reports the average size of selected regions.

claim: Only six genes occurred within the genomic regions under selection identified by hapFLK.
source: The average size of these regions was 16.7 kb and only six genes occurred within them.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of genes in selected regions.

claim: Each genomic region under selection identified by hapFLK included one to four strongly associated variants, all of which occurred in non-coding regions.
source: We used CAVIAR (Rochus et al., 2018) to identify variants showing strong associations with selection in these regions. Each region included one to four variants, all of which occurred in non-coding regions (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports CAVIAR results identifying strongly associated variants.

claim: Migration is the ancestral state in blackcaps.
source: Previous phylogeographic work suggested that migration is the ancestral state in blackcaps (Pérez-Tris et al., 2004; Voelker and Light, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous phylogeographic studies that established this conclusion.

claim: Selection in genomic regions identified in resident blackcaps is probably involved in the transition from migrant to resident phenotypes.
source: Accordingly, the selection in genomic regions that we identified here is probably involved in the transition from migrant to resident phenotypes.
evidence: The manuscript infers this based on the ancestral state being migratory and selection signals in residents.

claim: Eight of the nine regions identified by hapFLK also exhibited extreme values of ΔPBS and nSL in the same population.
source: Eight of the nine regions identified by hapFLK also exhibited extreme values of ΔPBS and nSL (in the top 1% of the distribution) in the same population as that identified by hapFLK (ΔPBS Table 1a, Figure 3b for resident birds [estimates for short distance SW, medium distance SE, SW, NW, and long distance SE, Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Figure 2—figure supplement 5; Figure 2—figure supplement 6]; nSL Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports concordance between multiple selection statistics.

claim: Two strongly associated SNPs identified by CAVIAR are located in the 3′ untranslated regions of GPR83-L and CHST4.
source: In support of this suggestion, an alignment of predicted mRNAs from several bird species and transcripts from a testis transcriptome of the blackcap placed two of the SNPs from CAVIAR in the 3′ untranslated region (3′ UTRs) of two genes (GPR83-L on Super-Scaffold 12 and CHST4 on Super-Scaffold 13, syntenic with flycatcher chromosomes 11 and 4a, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports the location of specific SNPs based on sequence alignment.

claim: 3′ UTRs can act as posttranscriptional regulators by containing binding sites for microRNAs.
source: Three prime3′ UTRs can act as posttranscriptional regulators; they contain binding sides for microRNAs, which can inhibit translation or target mRNA for degradation (Mayr, 2017; Barrett et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the regulatory function of 3′ UTRs.

claim: 55 conserved microRNAs are differentially expressed between summer and migratory monarch butterflies.
source: In fact, previous work with monarch butterflies identified 55 conserved microRNAs that are differentially expressed between summer and migratory butterflies (Zhan et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on microRNA expression in monarch butterflies.

claim: A bHLH motif (GHCACGTG) was found on Super-Scaffolds 12 and 99 in genomic regions under selection in resident blackcaps.
source: We found a bHLH motif (GHCACGTG) on Super-Scaffolds 12 and 99 (Figures 3a,b, 4a and 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports finding this transcription factor binding motif using HOMER.

claim: A SNP (G/T) at the beginning of the bHLH motif on Super-Scaffold 99 is nearly fixed in continental resident blackcaps.
source: The motif on Super-Scaffold 99 is particularly interesting as there is a SNP (G/T) at the beginning of the motif that is nearly fixed in continental residents (the allele frequency for G in Asni, Gibraltar and Cazalla de la Sierra is 1, 0.85 and 0.9, respectively; FST between Gibraltar and medium-distance NW, SW and SE migratory populations is 0.15, 0.25 and 0.44, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports allele frequencies and FST values for this specific SNP.

claim: Clock, Npas2 and Bmal1 are involved in maintaining circadian rhythms.
source: Clock, Npas2 and Bmal1 are involved in maintaining circadian rhythms.
evidence: The manuscript states the function of these genes.

claim: Circadian rhythms synchronize circannual clocks, which are important cues controlling seasonal migratory behaviour.
source: Circadian rhythms synchronize circannual clocks, which are important cues controlling seasonal migratory behaviour (Gwinner, 1996; Visser et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the relationship between circadian rhythms and migration.

claim: LOC100859173 has been annotated as a probable G-protein coupled receptor that mediates the function of neuropeptide Y (NPY).
source: For example, LOC100859173 (located on in the genomic region under selection on Super-Scaffold 12, the region with a bHLH motif mentioned above; Table 1a) has been annotated as a probable G-protein coupled receptor that mediates the function of neuropeptide Y (NPY).
evidence: The manuscript reports the annotation of this gene.

claim: NPY is localized in the brain of birds and works with AGRP and POMC to control energy balance.
source: NPY is localized in the brain of birds and works with Agouti-related peptide (AGRP) and proopiomelanocortin (POMC) to control energy balance.
evidence: The manuscript describes the function and localization of NPY.

claim: NPY/AGRP neurons stimulate appetite, food intake and fat deposition, while POMC inhibits these processes.
source: Specifically, NPY/AGRP neurons stimulate appetite, food intake and fat deposition, while POMC inhibits these processes (Boswell and Dunn, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the function of these neural pathways.

claim: The effects of NPY may extend to seasonal changes in energy balance important for migration, including hyperphagia and fat deposition.
source: It has been hypothesized that the effects of NPY may extend to seasonal changes in energy balance that are important for migration, including hyperphagia and fat deposition (Boswell and Dunn, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a hypothesis about NPY's role in migration.

claim: NPY facilitates learning and memory via the modulation of hippocampal activity and has an effect on circadian rhythms, reproduction, and the contraction of vascular smooth muscles.
source: Beyond its role in energy balance, NPY also facilitates learning and memory via the modulation of hippocampal activity and has an effect on circadian rhythms, reproduction, and the contraction of vascular smooth muscles.
evidence: The manuscript describes multiple functions of NPY.

claim: Six genomic regions under positive selection were identified by hapFLK in an analysis limited to medium-distance migrants with varying orientations.
source: Starting with orientation and limiting our analysis to medium-distance migrants with varying orientations (medium-distance NW, SW and SE migrants, total number of birds included in these analyses = 54, Supplementary file 4), hapFLK identified only six regions that are under positive selection (Table 1b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of regions under selection in the orientation analysis.

claim: Most genomic regions under selection in the orientation analysis showed selection in the NW phenotype.
source: Most of these regions showed selection in the NW phenotype and exhibited extreme values of ΔPBS limited to the population identified by hapFLK (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: The manuscript describes the distribution of selection signals across phenotypes.

claim: SDC1 codes for a transmembrane protein that helps to regulate the Wnt signalling pathway.
source: For example, SDC1 is a region on Super-Scaffold_17 that is under selection in NW migrants. This gene codes for a transmembrane protein that helps to regulate the Wnt signalling pathway.
evidence: The manuscript describes the function of SDC1.

claim: The Wnt signalling pathway plays a role in embryonic development and has been shown to influence feather and beak morphogenesis, along with feather molt.
source: This pathway plays a role in embryonic development and has been shown to influence feather and beak morphogenesis, along with feather molt (Yu et al., 2004; Mallarino et al., 2011; Bhullar et al., 2015; Widelitz, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the function of the Wnt pathway.

claim: NW migrant blackcaps have rounder wings and more narrow beaks than southern migrants.
source: NW migrants have rounder wings and more narrow beaks than southern migrants (Rolshausen et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study documenting morphological differences.

claim: Variation in molt patterns has been documented between NW migrants and birds that are resident on the continent.
source: This has not been evaluated directly in comparisons between migrants, but variation in molt patterns have been documented between NW migrants and birds that are resident on the continent (de la Hera et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on molt patterns.

claim: Delmore and Liedvogel (2016) identified a genomic region on chromosome 4 associated with orientation in Swainson's thrushes.
source: Delmore and Liedvogel (2016) identified a region on chromosome 4 and Lundberg et al. (2017) regions on chromosome 1 and 5 that are associated with orientation.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on the genomics of orientation.

claim: Lundberg et al. (2017) identified genomic regions on chromosomes 1 and 5 associated with orientation in willow warblers.
source: Delmore and Liedvogel (2016) identified a region on chromosome 4 and Lundberg et al. (2017) regions on chromosome 1 and 5 that are associated with orientation.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on the genomics of orientation.

claim: None of the genomic regions associated with orientation in blackcaps overlap with those identified in Swainson's thrushes or willow warblers.
source: None of these regions overlap with those under selection in our study on blackcaps.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the lack of overlap between studies.

claim: Several studies have failed to document an association between migration and Clock.
source: Nevertheless, several studies have failed to document an association with Clock, and a comparison of our results with those of Delmore and Liedvogel (2016) and Lundberg et al. (2017) adds further caution to this idea of a common basis (at least at the sequence level).
evidence: The manuscript references multiple studies that did not find associations with Clock.

claim: None of the genomic regions identified by hapFLK and PBS were fixed for alternate haplotypes or alleles.
source: None of the regions identified by hapFLK and PBS were fixed for alternate haplotypes or alleles. This fact is evident in Figure 4, in which the regions under selection still include haplotypes from a different cluster
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4 as evidence.

claim: Selection is acting on shared genetic variation in blackcaps rather than newly derived mutations.
source: This fact is evident in Figure 4, in which the regions under selection still include haplotypes from a different cluster, and it could suggest that selection is acting on shared genetic variation (i.e., variation that is already present in the population rather than newly derived mutations).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the haplotype patterns observed.

claim: Shared genetic variation can facilitate rapid transitions between migratory phenotypes as these variants are already present in the population and have been tested by selection.
source: Shared variation can facilitate these rapid changes as these variants are already present in the population and have been tested by selection (Barrett and Schluter, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the role of standing variation in rapid evolution.

claim: The narrow size of genomic regions under selection supports a role for shared genetic variation.
source: The fact that regions under selection are quite narrow (Table 1) also supports a role for shared genetic variation (Barrett and Schluter, 2008)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature linking narrow selection regions to standing variation.

claim: Genetic distance from the ancestral sequence was similar for haplotypes from all clusters in the region on Super-Scaffold 73 under selection in NW migrants.
source: This is precisely what we found; genetic distance from the ancestral sequence was similar for haplotypes from all clusters (181 differences for the NW haplotype vs. 178, 179 and 181 [x3] and 182 differences in the rest).
evidence: The manuscript reports genetic distance calculations from ancestral sequences.

claim: Six synonymous substitutions were identified between all three medium-distance migrant populations and both garden warblers and hill babblers in coding regions of ATG2B and BDKDB.
source: Specifically, we identified six synonymous substitutions between all three medium-distance migrant populations and both garden warblers and hill babblers, suggesting that there is no difference in the age of these haplotypes.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of synonymous substitutions found.

claim: Garden warblers were more closely related to blackcaps than were hill babblers in the phylogenetic tree built using data from the region on Super-Scaffold 73.
source: By contrast, garden warblers were more closely related to blackcaps than were hill babblers in the tree built using data from the region on Super-Scaffold 73 (Figure 6b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the phylogenetic relationships in the gene tree.

claim: The medium-distance NW population occurs at the base of the blackcap clade in the phylogenetic tree built using data from Super-Scaffold 73.
source: In addition, the medium-distance NW population (in which positive selection is acting in this particular region) occurs at the base of the blackcap clade.
evidence: The manuscript describes the position of NW migrants in the gene tree.

claim: Garden warblers are obligate migrants.
source: Recall that garden warblers are obligate migrants whereas hill babblers are residents
evidence: The manuscript states the migratory status of garden warblers.

claim: Hill babblers are resident birds.
source: Recall that garden warblers are obligate migrants whereas hill babblers are residents
evidence: The manuscript states the migratory status of hill babblers.

claim: The site frequency spectrum for the region on Super-Scaffold 73 shows an excess of mid-frequency alleles compared to random genomic sequences.
source: SFSs for the random sequences are similar to expectations under neutrality, with a preponderance of alleles at low frequencies. By contrast, the SFS of Super-Scaffold 73 shows an excess of mid-frequency alleles (Figure 6c).
evidence: The manuscript compares the SFS of the selected region to random sequences.

claim: Greater variance in site frequency spectra is expected when selection makes use of standing variation because alleles have been recombining onto different backgrounds in ancestral populations.
source: Greater variance in SFSs are expected when selection makes use of standing variation because alleles have been recombining onto different backgrounds in ancestral populations (Przeworski et al., 2005; Pennings and Hermisson, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the expected SFS patterns under selection on standing variation.

claim: A large percentage of variance in migratory distance can be explained by the SNP set (PVE = 0.90 ± 0.28).
source: Our results suggest that a large percentage of variance in migratory distance can be explained by our SNP set (PVE = 0.90 ± 0.28), but only one SNP showed a strong association with this focal trait (posterior inclusion probability >0.01).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of variance explained from BSLMM analysis.

claim: Only one SNP showed a strong association with migratory distance (posterior inclusion probability >0.01).
source: Our results suggest that a large percentage of variance in migratory distance can be explained by our SNP set (PVE = 0.90 ± 0.28), but only one SNP showed a strong association with this focal trait (posterior inclusion probability >0.01).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of strongly associated SNPs from BSLMM analysis.

claim: The SNP strongly associated with migratory distance is located on Super-Scaffold 79 and is 627-bp downstream from the gene KCNIP1.
source: This SNP is located on Super-Scaffold 79, occurs in an area of elevated FST between long- and short-distance migrants (FST = 0.31, in 0.018 percentile FST values) and is 627-bp downstream from the gene KCNIP1, which encodes a potassium channel interacting protein (major determinants of neuronal cell excitability).
evidence: The manuscript reports the location and context of the SNP associated with distance.

claim: KCNIP1 encodes a potassium channel interacting protein that is a major determinant of neuronal cell excitability.
source: This SNP is located on Super-Scaffold 79, occurs in an area of elevated FST between long- and short-distance migrants (FST = 0.31, in 0.018 percentile FST values) and is 627-bp downstream from the gene KCNIP1, which encodes a potassium channel interacting protein (major determinants of neuronal cell excitability).
evidence: The manuscript describes the function of KCNIP1.

claim: The propensity to migrate, orientation and distance of migration all map to a small number of genomic regions.
source: The propensity to migrate, orientation and distance of migration all map to a small number of genomic regions that do not overlap with results from other species, suggesting that there are multiple ways to generate variation in migration.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings on the genetic architecture of migration traits.

claim: Genomic regions associated with migration traits in blackcaps do not overlap with results from other species.
source: The propensity to migrate, orientation and distance of migration all map to a small number of genomic regions that do not overlap with results from other species, suggesting that there are multiple ways to generate variation in migration.
evidence: The manuscript compares results across species and notes lack of overlap.

claim: There are multiple ways to generate variation in migration.
source: The propensity to migrate, orientation and distance of migration all map to a small number of genomic regions that do not overlap with results from other species, suggesting that there are multiple ways to generate variation in migration.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the lack of overlap in genomic regions across species.

claim: Strongly associated SNPs were located in regulatory regions of candidate genes that may serve as major regulators of the migratory syndrome.
source: Strongly associated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were located in regulatory regions of candidate genes that may serve as major regulators of the migratory syndrome.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings on SNP locations and their potential regulatory roles.

claim: Evidence for selection on shared variation was documented in blackcaps.
source: Evidence for selection on shared variation was documented, providing a mechanism by which rapid changes may evolve.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes evidence for selection on standing variation.

claim: Selection on shared variation provides a mechanism by which rapid changes in migration may evolve.
source: Evidence for selection on shared variation was documented, providing a mechanism by which rapid changes may evolve.
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism from the evidence of selection on standing variation.

claim: European blackcaps exhibit dramatic differences in migratory behaviour, spanning the entire spectrum from exclusively migratory populations in the northern portion of their range to resident populations.
source: Blackcaps exhibit dramatic differences in migratory behaviour (Figure 1a), spanning the entire spectrum from exclusively migratory populations in the northern portion of their range to short distance and partially migratory populations in the Mediterranean; non-migratory, or resident, populations occur on both the European continent (Iberian Peninsula) and the Atlantic islands.
evidence: The manuscript describes the range of migratory behaviors in blackcaps.

claim: A migratory divide occurs in blackcaps between populations that migrate southwest and southeast from their breeding grounds in Central Europe.
source: In addition to variation in the propensity to migrate and the distance covered, blackcaps vary in migratory orientation, with a migratory divide (contact zone between populations that breed adjacent to one another but take different migratory routes) occurring between populations that migrate southwest (SW) and southeast (SE) from their breeding grounds in Central Europe in the autumn.
evidence: The manuscript describes the migratory divide in blackcaps.

claim: A novel northwest migratory route evolved very recently in blackcaps, with an increasing number of birds migrating northwest from Central European breeding grounds.
source: A novel migratory route also evolved very recently in this species, with an increasing number of birds migrating northwest (NW) from the Central European breeding grounds in the autumn (Cramp, 1992).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the recent evolution of the NW route.

claim: Common garden experiments showed that selectively bred blackcaps reared in isolation from their parents maintain population-specific migratory behaviour.
source: Common garden experiments showed that selectively bred individuals that were reared in isolation from their parents maintain population-specific behaviour, suggesting that there is a genetic component to migration (Helbig, 1994; Helbig et al., 1989; Helbig, 1991a; Berthold and Querner, 1981; Pulido and Berthold, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies demonstrating genetic control of migration.

claim: F1 hybrids crossbred between blackcap populations that differ in migratory traits exhibited intermediate phenotypes.
source: F1 hybrids crossbred between populations that differ in migratory traits exhibited intermediate phenotypes (orientation, distance and propensity to migrate), suggesting that these traits are additively inherited (Berthold and Querner, 1981; Pulido and Berthold, 2010; Helbig, 1991b).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on hybrid phenotypes.

claim: Migratory traits in blackcaps are additively inherited.
source: F1 hybrids crossbred between populations that differ in migratory traits exhibited intermediate phenotypes (orientation, distance and propensity to migrate), suggesting that these traits are additively inherited (Berthold and Querner, 1981; Pulido and Berthold, 2010; Helbig, 1991b).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies that inferred additive inheritance from hybrid phenotypes.

claim: F2 hybrids of blackcaps showed a wider distribution of phenotypes and the recovery of parental phenotypes, indicative of traits controlled by only a few major genes.
source: Further work with F2 hybrids showed a wider distribution of phenotypes and the recovery of parental phenotypes, indicative of traits that are controlled by only a few major genes (Helbig, 1996)
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on F2 hybrids and genetic architecture.

claim: Selection experiments mating blackcaps according to migratory status showed that the transition between resident and migratory behaviour can occur in just a few generations.
source: selection experiments mating birds according to migratory status showed that the transition between resident and migratory behaviour can occur in just a few generations (Pulido et al., 1996; Berthold et al., 1990).
evidence: The manuscript cites selection experiments demonstrating rapid evolution.

claim: The northwest migratory route in blackcaps was only established in the past 70 years and probably in response to increased food availability during winter in the United Kingdom.
source: The rapidity with which migratory behaviour can evolve has been supported in natural populations; the NW route taken by some birds was only established in the past 70 years and probably in response to increased food availability during the winter in the United Kingdom (Berthold et al., 1992).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the recent evolution of the NW route.

claim: Pérez-Tris et al. (2004) used mitochondrial control region data from 241 birds and 12 populations to show that migratory variation in blackcaps arose recently (4,000–13,000 years ago).
source: Pérez-Tris et al. (2004) used mitochondrial (control) data from 241 birds and 12 populations across the entire breeding range to show that migratory variation in this species arose recently (4,000–13,000 years ago [ya]) and has not yet resulted in significant population differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript cites a phylogeographic study on blackcaps.

claim: Migratory variation in blackcaps has not yet resulted in significant population differentiation according to mitochondrial data.
source: Pérez-Tris et al. (2004) used mitochondrial (control) data from 241 birds and 12 populations across the entire breeding range to show that migratory variation in this species arose recently (4,000–13,000 years ago [ya]) and has not yet resulted in significant population differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from a phylogeographic study.

claim: The only blackcap populations showing substantial genetic differentiation in mitochondrial data occurred in the Central European migratory divide between SW and SE migrants.
source: The only populations showing substantial genetic differentiation occurred in the Central European migratory divide (i.e., between SW and SE migrants), indicating that differences in orientation may help to maintain population differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from a phylogeographic study.

claim: Differences in migratory orientation may help to maintain population differentiation in blackcaps.
source: The only populations showing substantial genetic differentiation occurred in the Central European migratory divide (i.e., between SW and SE migrants), indicating that differences in orientation may help to maintain population differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript cites an inference from a phylogeographic study.

claim: Resident blackcap populations showed evidence of historical bottlenecks followed by sudden expansions.
source: Resident populations showed evidence of historical bottlenecks followed by sudden expansions, suggesting that blackcaps lost their ability to migrate after secondary colonization of mild areas in southern Europe and on the Atlantic islands.
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from a phylogeographic study.

claim: Blackcaps lost their ability to migrate after secondary colonization of mild areas in southern Europe and on the Atlantic islands.
source: Resident populations showed evidence of historical bottlenecks followed by sudden expansions, suggesting that blackcaps lost their ability to migrate after secondary colonization of mild areas in southern Europe and on the Atlantic islands.
evidence: The manuscript cites an inference from a phylogeographic study.

claim: Voelker and Light (2011) used mitochondrial ND2 and cytb data to reconstruct ancestral states within the genus Sylvia.
source: This finding was supported by Voelker and Light (2011) who used mitochondrial (ND2 and cytb) data to reconstruct ancestral states within the genus Sylvia.
evidence: The manuscript cites a phylogenetic study.

claim: Dietzen et al. (2008) documented limited genetic differentiation between blackcaps using mitochondrial cytb data.
source: Limited genetic differentiation between blackcaps was also documented by Dietzen et al. (2008) using mitochondrial (cytb) data
evidence: The manuscript cites a phylogeographic study.

claim: Colonization of the Canary Islands occurred 300,000–3,000,000 years ago while colonization of other Atlantic islands including the Azores and Cape Verde occurred 4,000–40,000 years ago.
source: these authors also estimated dates for the colonization of Atlantic islands and for an earlier colonisation of the Canary Islands (the latter occurring 300,000–3,000,000 ya vs. 4,000–40,000 ya for colonisation of other islands including the Azores and Cape Verde).
evidence: The manuscript cites colonization dates from Dietzen et al. (2008).

claim: Differentiation remains low between migratory blackcap populations despite divergence beginning approximately 30,000 years ago.
source: Populations of blackcaps began to diverge ~30,000 years ago, but differentiation remains low between migratory populations.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes demographic findings.

claim: There is evidence for past gene flow between migratory and resident blackcap populations on the European continent.
source: There is evidence for past gene flow between migratory and resident populations on the European continent but comparison of the contemporary structure of these populations suggests that gene flow may be limited.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes demographic findings.

claim: Contemporary gene flow may be limited between migratory and resident blackcap populations on the European continent.
source: There is evidence for past gene flow between migratory and resident populations on the European continent but comparison of the contemporary structure of these populations suggests that gene flow may be limited.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from population structure analysis.

claim: Gene flow is limited for resident island blackcap populations.
source: This is certainly the case for resident island birds.
evidence: The manuscript states this based on population structure results.

claim: No protein-coding change is shared across the three focal migratory traits (propensity, distance and orientation) examined in blackcaps.
source: We do not find evidence for one common genetic mechanism across species here, and no protein-coding change is shared across the three focal traits (propensity, distance and orientation) that we examined in unison.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings on the genetic architecture of migration.

claim: NPY and bHLH transcription factors are good candidates for major regulators that control multiple migratory traits.
source: Future work on gene expression may identify major regulators that control multiple migratory traits, and both NPY and bHLH transcription factors are good candidates.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on potential major regulators based on findings.

claim: Hybrids between blackcap populations with different migratory orientations exhibit intermediate orientation behaviour that is predicted to be inferior.
